title: Baba Dayal's Nirankaris today
hook: a reform movement distinct from the later Sant Nirankari Mission

segments.voice: Yesterday's lesson, the Namdharis today, met white dress, simple rites, and a living guru. Your line was different, and respected. Whose difference did you say the way they'd say it? Day one thousand three hundred fifteen.

Two restaurants in one city share a name. One is a family place that has served the same dish for generations. The other opened later, with a different menu and a different owner. Locals never mix them up. Visitors do it all the time, and the family place keeps having to explain: that's not us. Sikh history has a pair like that. Two movements carry the word Nirankari. They are not the same, and today is about telling them apart, carefully and fairly.
screen: `TWO PLACES, ONE NAME.` → `LOCALS NEVER MIX THEM UP.` → `TWO NIRANKARI MOVEMENTS.`

segments.voice: Start with the word. Nirankar means the Formless One, a name for God that runs through Gurbani. In the Japji, from Ang 3, Guru Nanak closes several stanzas with a refrain, here in paraphrase: you are forever safe and whole, O Formless One. To be a Nirankari is to belong to the Formless. Now the first movement. Baba Dayal was a Sikh reformer in the northwest of Punjab, in the city of Rawalpindi. Tradition remembers him calling Sikhs back to the Formless One and away from rites he saw creeping in: idols, priestly ceremonies, customs that pulled attention from the Guru's word. His movement is especially remembered for weddings. Nirankaris married by circling the Guru Granth Sahib while the Lavan, Guru Ram Das's wedding hymns, were sung. That's the anand karaj, the wedding rite Sikhs know today. Baba Dayal's Nirankaris continue as a community that honors the Guru Granth Sahib and remembers its founder. Now the second movement. The Sant Nirankari Mission is a later and separate organization, with its own living leaders and its own teachings. Sikh bodies have been in serious, painful disagreement with it. That story is heavy, and it deserves more than one sentence in a short lesson, so this path leaves it there. Here's why the distinction matters. When the two are confused, a reform remembered for the wedding around the Granth gets tangled up with a conflict it had no part in. Knowing the difference is a small act of fairness to both.
screen: `NIRANKAR: THE FORMLESS ONE.` · `BABA DAYAL: BACK TO THE FORMLESS.` · `THE WEDDING AROUND THE GRANTH.` · `A LATER, SEPARATE MISSION.` · then, large: `KNOW THE DIFFERENCE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: learn one distinction. Settle, and breathe. Say the two names to yourself once, slowly: Baba Dayal's Nirankaris; the Sant Nirankari Mission. Then attach one plain fact to the first: the reformer, and the wedding around the Granth. Attach one plain fact to the second: later, and separate. Breathe in on the first name, out on the second, and let them sit apart in your mind like two houses on different streets. If you pray, you can rest on Nirankar, the Formless One. The bell holds the time.

Baba Dayal's Nirankaris today. A reform movement that called Sikhs back to the Formless One and is remembered for weddings around the Granth. Separate from the later Sant Nirankari Mission. Today's word.

Your line: know the difference. Today, catch one place where two things with the same name, two people, two groups, two ideas, are being mixed up, and quietly set them straight, at least in your own head. Day one thousand three hundred fifteen.
